clue.text: Yearns for T-shirts

indicators.note: 'for' read as 'in exchange for': the garment's letters are swapped round into a new order

parts.note: the clue word's own letters, hyphen dropped

explanation.surface: Someone pines after a new set of casual tops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' is the only signal: the letters of T-SHIRTS are taken in exchange for a rearrangement of themselves, giving THIRSTS.
explanation.definitionFit: To yearn is to long eagerly, and one who thirsts likewise craves something keenly.

clue.text: Milton's unexpected contribution to the orchestra

definitions.text: Milton's unexpected contribution to the orchestra

parts.words: Milton's unexpected contribution to the orchestra
parts.note: Wordsworth's sonnet 'Scorn not the Sonnet' says that in Milton's hand the sonnet became a brass instrument, from which he blew soul-animating strains

explanation.surface: The poet of Paradise Lost apparently wrote a part for the band.
explanation.walkthrough: Wordsworth wrote of the sonnet that in Milton's hand 'The Thing became a trumpet'; the clue treats that as if Milton had added an instrument to the orchestra.
explanation.definitionFit: A brass instrument with valves is a standard member of an orchestra, and Wordsworth's line hands one to Milton.

clue.text: Facial adornments with a deceptively simple air

indicators.note: the words appear simple but are deceiving us: their letters must be reshuffled

explanation.surface: Beards worn with an innocent look that hides cunning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deceptively' tells you to rearrange SIMPLE AIR into IMPERIALS.
explanation.definitionFit: An imperial is a small pointed tuft of beard below the lower lip, named after Napoleon III.

clue.text: Youngster with whom one may come to grips

indicators.note: 'come to' in the sense of turning into: the word grips is rearranged to become something else

explanation.surface: A boy one can wrestle with.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests grappling, but 'come to' is the anagram signal on GRIPS.
explanation.definitionFit: A sprig is an old word for a young person, a scion of a family.

clue.text: Accoutrement of a Knight Bachelor?

parts.note: a bachelor knight is a 'Sir' who is single, and that sounds like the name of a horse's strap

explanation.surface: Asking what kit a particular grade of knight carries.
explanation.walkthrough: A Knight Bachelor is a real British honour, the lowest grade of knighthood; read as 'Sir single' it suggests the girth strap that goes round a horse.
explanation.definitionFit: A surcingle is a belt passing round a horse's body, part of the gear of a mounted knight.

clue.text: Speaker from Boston appears well padded

definitions.meaning: an orator on the stump, a political speaker, here an American one; Boston in Lincolnshire also has a church tower called the Stump
a cricket wicketkeeper, who wears thick leg pads

explanation.surface: An American orator looks rather portly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'well padded' suggests plumpness but means wearing cricket pads: a stumper is a wicketkeeper.
explanation.definitionFit: One who stumps makes speeches on the hustings, and in cricket the stumper keeps wicket in heavy pads.

clue.text: Here he is, up perhaps among the more popular composers"

definitions.note: a phrase standing for one member of that group, a noun

indicators.note: 'Here' points at the very words that follow, which hold the name inside them

explanation.surface: A composer is pointed out, perhaps on the way up the popularity charts.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'iS UP PErhaps'.
explanation.definitionFit: Franz von Suppé wrote light operettas and overtures such as Light Cavalry, long staples of popular concerts.

clue.text: " And suns and —— ceased to be " (E. Brontë)

definitions.text: " And suns and —— ceased to be " (E. Brontë)

parts.words: " And suns and —— ceased to be " (E. Brontë)
parts.note: a line from Emily Brontë's poem 'No coward soul is mine' with one word blanked out for the solver to supply

explanation.walkthrough: The full line is 'And suns and universes ceased to be', from Emily Brontë's last poem.
explanation.definitionFit: Brontë pairs suns with whole cosmic systems, the plural of the totality of all that exists.

clue.text: Where to find St. James's (R.C. Church, W.1 ?

definitions.text: Where to find St. James's (R.C. Church, W.1 ?

parts.words: Where to find St. James's (R.C. Church, W.1 ?
parts.note: the Roman Catholic church of St James in London W1 stands in Spanish Place, so the answer is a Spanish word for a place or square

explanation.surface: A request for directions to a London Catholic church.
explanation.walkthrough: St James's, Spanish Place, is a Catholic church in Marylebone, central London; 'Spanish place' is turned into the Spanish word for a public square.
explanation.definitionFit: In Spanish towns the open public square is called by this word, so a Spanish place.

clue.text: Revolutionary guide ?

parts.note: red is the colour of revolutionaries and communists
a book can be a guide or handbook

explanation.surface: A handbook for would-be revolutionaries.
explanation.definitionFit: A red book is an official directory or handbook, and Mao's little red book was a revolutionary's manual.

clue.text: Only ten in the House ?

parts.note: the aristocracy, and the House of Lords is the higher chamber of Parliament

explanation.surface: Asking whether a parliamentary chamber has a tiny attendance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The upper ten (thousand)' is an old phrase for the aristocracy; the Lords is the Upper House.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes both the aristocratic 'ten' and the higher chamber of Parliament.

clue.text: It's deserved by an unruly rip in one kind of home

definitions.note: a phrase for something earned, standing for a noun

indicators.note: 'in' says the rearranged letters go inside the home

parts.note: a remand home was a British institution holding young offenders awaiting trial

indicators.note: an unruly thing is disorderly, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A tear made by a delinquent in a juvenile home earns a telling-off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unruly' turns RIP into PRI, which goes 'in' REMAND (a British remand home, where young offenders were held) to give RE-PRI-MAND.
explanation.definitionFit: A rebuke is what a wrongdoer has earned, a formal scolding.

clue.text: Pilgrim who travels by air

definitions.meaning: an old sense: a wanderer or traveller from foreign parts
a falcon, a bird of prey that flies

explanation.surface: A pilgrim who takes a plane.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests air travel; the second sense is the falcon.
explanation.definitionFit: The word comes from Latin for a foreigner or wayfarer, and it also names a swift falcon.

clue.text: Gifted girl seated in a Sheraton armchair

indicators.note: the girl sits inside the furniture-maker's name, its letters held within

explanation.surface: A talented young woman sitting in a fine Georgian chair.
explanation.walkthrough: The run is shERATOn. Sheraton was an 18th-century English furniture designer.
explanation.definitionFit: Erato is one of the nine Muses, of love poetry, a gifted inspiring goddess.

clue.text: A proverbially warm drink ?

parts.note: the saying 'as warm as' a slice of browned bread, and also the act of drinking to someone's health

explanation.surface: Asking for the name of a well-known hot beverage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Warm as toast' is the proverb; a toast is also a drink raised to someone.
explanation.definitionFit: Browned bread is proverbially warm, and raising glasses in honour of someone is drinking one.

clue.text: Robespierre found it particularly hot !

parts.note: the French Revolutionary calendar's month of heat, in which Robespierre was overthrown in 1794

explanation.surface: The revolutionary leader suffered in the heat.
explanation.walkthrough: The month's name comes from Greek for heat, and the coup of 9 of that month in 1794 sent Robespierre to the guillotine: things got hot for him.
explanation.definitionFit: The eleventh month of the French Republican calendar, high summer, named from the Greek word for warmth.

clue.text: In this case, the Colonel's baton !

definitions.text: In this case, the Colonel's baton !

parts.words: In this case, the Colonel's baton !
parts.note: the colonel of the Life Guards carries a ceremonial rod cased in precious metal, and the title is his

explanation.surface: Pointing to a display case holding an officer's baton.
explanation.walkthrough: Gold Stick is the title of the colonel of the Household Cavalry who attends the British sovereign, from the gilt-headed staff he carries; 'case' plays on the casing of gold.
explanation.definitionFit: The ceremonial staff of the royal bodyguard's colonel is gilded, giving both rod and officer their name.

clue.text: One was " Summoned by Bells "

parts.note: Dick Whittington heard the London bells call 'Turn again', foretelling his civic office in London

explanation.surface: Quoting the title of John Betjeman's verse autobiography.
explanation.walkthrough: Summoned by Bells is Betjeman's book, but here the bells are Bow Bells calling Dick Whittington back to become thrice the head of the City of London.
explanation.definitionFit: The head of the City of London's corporation, an office Whittington held three times after the bells recalled him.

clue.text: But is it ciné art to be so complex ?

indicators.note: the letters are invited to become something else, rearranged into a new word

parts.note: the clue words' own letters, accent dropped

explanation.surface: Asking whether film art really needs to be so complicated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be' signals that IT CINE ART rearranges; 'But is' and 'so' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Something intricate has many interwoven parts, hard to follow.

clue.text: Sam, although one, was not in a trio

definitions.text: Sam, although one, was not in a trio

parts.words: Sam, although one, was not in a trio
parts.note: Stanley Holloway's monologue soldier Sam, told to pick up his musket, carried that gun yet was no comrade of Dumas's famous three

explanation.surface: A man called Sam was never part of a threesome.
explanation.walkthrough: Sam Small, of the monologue 'Pick oop tha' musket', bore a musket, so was a musket-man, but Dumas's famous trio were Athos, Porthos and Aramis.
explanation.definitionFit: A soldier armed with an old smooth-bore gun, the title of Dumas's famous trio.

clue.text: Islander registers vote between two identical males

indicators.note: the vote is placed between the pair, splitting them
the male is given twice over

parts.note: a man is a male
X is the cross marked on a ballot

explanation.surface: An islander records his ballot between two lookalike men.
explanation.walkthrough: 'two identical' doubles MAN, and 'between' puts X in the middle; 'registers' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of the Isle of Man, in the Irish Sea.

clue.text: Begin a career in the lead at Wimbledon

definitions.meaning: to establish oneself, as in business
a tennis player ahead by a set; Wimbledon is the London tennis championship

explanation.surface: Starting out professionally while leading a tennis match.
explanation.walkthrough: Wimbledon is the famous tennis tournament held in south-west London.
explanation.definitionFit: To establish oneself in a trade, and to be one set ahead in a tennis match.

clue.text: A sleep's indicated, so gratifying

definitions.note: an adjective; the verb form 'is gratifying' fits the answer

indicators.note: the letters are pointing to another word, read in a different order

parts.note: the clue words' own letters with the possessive S kept as a letter

explanation.surface: A nap is recommended, which is welcome news.
explanation.walkthrough: 'indicated' signals the anagram of A SLEEP'S, keeping the S.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that delights or satisfies someone is gratifying them.

clue.text: Turkish soldier in Hyderabad

definitions.meaning: a regular soldier in the Ottoman army
the title of the ruler of the Indian princely state of Hyderabad

explanation.surface: An Ottoman soldier stationed in India.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses come from an Arabic word for order: an Ottoman regular trooper, and the governing prince of Hyderabad.

clue.text: Animal writing ? It's on the up-and-up

parts.note: a zoo is an animal collection
MS is the abbreviation for manuscript, a piece of writing

explanation.surface: Is animal-themed literature becoming more popular?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Animal' stands for ZOO, a place of animals, attributively.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that zooms climbs steeply and fast, rising ever higher.

clue.text: Wherein performers should know the ropes

definitions.text: Wherein performers should know the ropes

parts.words: Wherein performers should know the ropes
parts.note: bell-ringers pull ropes in a church tower, so the performers are ringers and the ropes are literal

explanation.surface: Describing a theatre where actors must be experienced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'know the ropes' suggests being experienced; the ropes here are bell ropes in a tower.
explanation.definitionFit: A freestanding bell tower, where ringers work the bell ropes.

clue.text: Distinguished companion taken bad with a cold

parts.note: CH stands for Companion of Honour, a British order
ill means bad, as in ill luck

explanation.surface: An eminent friend is laid low with a cold.
explanation.walkthrough: CH, Companion of Honour, is a British honour; 'taken' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A chill is a mild feverish cold caught from exposure.

clue.text: Jason's craft making for the north gas-powered ?

indicators.note: the ship heads towards the north, so N is placed after it

parts.note: the Argo was the ship of Jason and the Argonauts
N is the abbreviation for north

explanation.surface: The Argonauts' ship heading north under engine power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'making for' puts N after ARGO; 'powered' is surface padding attached to the definition 'gas'.
explanation.definitionFit: Argon is an inert noble gas found in air.

clue.text: Wander aimlessly about with Miss Bell for a flower ?

parts.note: to moon about is to wander listlessly
Daisy Bell is the girl in the song 'Daisy, Daisy' about a bicycle built for two

explanation.surface: Wandering about with a young lady to pick a flower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' is a link; Daisy Bell is the heroine of the old music-hall song 'Daisy, Daisy, give me your answer do'.
explanation.definitionFit: The moon-daisy, or ox-eye daisy, is a large white wild flower.

clue.text: The substance of 'Whitman's leaves

parts.note: Walt Whitman's collection is titled 'Leaves of' a green plant

explanation.surface: Asking what Whitman's pages are made of.
explanation.walkthrough: Whitman's poetry book is Leaves of Grass; 'leaves' looks like pages.
explanation.definitionFit: The plant whose blades form Whitman's title, a lawn's green covering.

clue.text: Respirator ?

parts.note: not a mask or machine but a natural opening through which one breathes

explanation.walkthrough: 'Respirator' suggests a breathing machine; the question mark points to the nose's own opening.
explanation.definitionFit: Each opening of the nose takes in air, so serves as a body part for breathing.

clue.text: Scarlet messengers

parts.note: scarlet bean plants bear the same name as people who carry messages

explanation.walkthrough: Scarlet runners are climbing beans; runners are also messengers.
explanation.definitionFit: Messengers who carry news on foot, and the beans called scarlet ones.
